title.en: Quadruped torso, limb stance and ground support

summary: Organize a four-legged character around separate shoulder and pelvic masses, named limb chains and an explicit support footprint rather than four oscillating rods.
objective: Make a quadruped recognizable in still pose and keep accepted body travel, limb stride and ground clearance consistent through start, stop and turn.
example_prompts: Design a stylized canine with visible pelvis, shoulders and paws, then explain what its walk animation actually controls.
Build a toy quadruped whose feet stop cycling when navigation is blocked.

principles: Choose a species reference or declare a fictional body plan before selecting paw, hoof or sole contact. The cited canine example is digitigrade; it does not establish the posture of bears, horses or every four-legged creature.
Separate the ribcage, pelvic mass, neck base and tail root so limb attachments have a place in the silhouette. Authored proportions can be caricatured without making all limbs identical.

Body navigation, joint posing and contact adjustment have different responsibilities. A gait-shaped display can suggest locomotion without calculating muscle forces or dynamically balancing the animal.
Use a foot-search region based on the actual limb reach and foot geometry; a tail or antler collision envelope is not the same thing as a supporting foot region.
implementation: Create named torso, pelvis, shoulder region, neck/head and tail groups; attach separate left/right forelimb and hindlimb chains. Store segment lengths, rest transforms and chosen joint bounds independently of skin meshes.

Block the limbs in side and front views before adding fur. Give each foot a sole/contact patch and readable toe or hoof termination; use a species reference for anatomical labels rather than calling every rear bend a knee.

For controlled locomotion, keep body position, velocity, heading, path, status and gait phase authoritative. Advance phase from accepted horizontal distance divided by authored stride length; scale limb excursion with actual speed and stop it at rest.

If stance locking is promised, save world-space stance targets and solve bounded limb reach against accepted support. Otherwise label the cyclic posing as approximate and inspect residual sliding; do not advertise foot locking from sinusoidal joints.

Use full rendered swept envelopes for obstacles, and separate foot probes for support. Reject unsafe steps before measuring travel. Bound turning speed, reserve a brief authored goal rest and restore all body, path, gait and animation-clock state on reset.
Choose overlapping rigid pieces, skinning or another deformation method that fits the style. Fur direction, nose finish and paw-pad material can clarify parts; shader roughness does not set friction.
observable_checks: At zero accepted travel, limb phase holds and walking amplitude reaches zero; a tail idle gesture may continue independently.
On a turn and a blocked step, no unsupported body displacement is counted as stride; joints remain attached at declared travel limits.
Inspect front, side and underside views: four intended contact regions are identifiable and decorative appendages remain within their separate collision envelope.
Reset during motion and compare pose, position, velocity, phase, path and timers with the initial snapshot.

known_limits: The canine source supports digitigrade contact only; proportions, speed, gait sequence and joint limits need species-specific evidence if presented as measured biology.
A support footprint and kinematic gait are not a balance controller, veterinary assessment or ground-reaction-force solution.
Authored modeling guidance and prospective checks; no runtime artifact has been executed for this record.
creative_affordances: Use stocky, elongated, mechanical or fantastical proportions; retain explicit contacts and state ownership when the creature shares space with obstacles.

claims.statement: The University of Minnesota canine skeleton teaching plate identifies canine ground contact as digitigrade.
claims.scope: Canine posture in the cited teaching plate; no extrapolation to all quadrupeds or quantitative locomotion.
